claims.text: Explicitly incorporating lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations into simulations will yield significantly more accurate low-phonon-thermal-conductivity predictions than empirical or conventional ab initio methods.
The targeted HEAs are random multielement solid solutions with substantial atomic-scale lattice distortions and chemical fluctuations.
A framework combining machine-learned force fields, ab initio molecular dynamics, and Boltzmann transport theory can account for lattice distortion and force-constant or chemical-bond fluctuations.
Disorder-related phonon scattering is pronounced in the 300–700 K range.
The approach is applicable primarily to HEAs containing typically five or more elements and having significant structural disorder.
Force-constant fluctuations in the relevant HEAs are on the order of 20–50%.
Lattice distortion reduces phonon velocity and enhances phonon scattering.
Force-constant fluctuations scatter and attenuate acoustic phonons in FeCoCrMnNi.
Chemical-bond variability contributes to lattice thermal conductivity by adding disorder-related scattering effects.
Reduced phonon velocity and increased scattering lower lattice thermal conductivity.
Current empirical or conventional DFT-only approaches do not fully capture disorder-induced phonon scattering in HEAs.
The proposed framework will reduce prediction error by at least 30% relative to conventional empirical or DFT-only approaches.
The approach's accuracy may diminish for weakly distorted materials, binary or ternary systems, and systems dominated by long-range order.
Prediction improvement may depend on alloy composition, parameter calibration, and simulation supercell size.
Laser-flash analysis and inelastic neutron scattering can independently determine the phonon thermal conductivity of the test alloys.
TEM and XRD can validate the magnitudes of lattice distortion and force-constant fluctuations.
Deviation of more than 20% from experiment across 300–700 K, when not explained by calibration uncertainty or experimental error, would falsify the hypothesis.
